planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kris Plant is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kris Plant is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Deeply cut, arrow-shaped leaves with pronounced wavy, serrated edges are glossy dark green with bold silvery-white veins and a metallic sheen, the jagged leaf margin giving the plant its common name after the wavy-bladed Southeast Asian kris dagger. Native to the Philippines and considered vulnerable in the wild due to habitat loss, it is a striking specimen for a shaded, humid patio or bright bathroom, its deeply lobed leaf shape distinguishing it at a glance from the broader, more solid-edged leaves of other commonly grown alocasias. Provide high humidity, protect from direct hot sun which scorches the leaves, and expect the plant to go dormant and lose its leaves if temperatures drop much below 55°F, resprouting from the rhizome once warmth returns.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Purple Sword alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Purple Sword alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Long, narrow, elongated leaves with distinctly scalloped, undulating margins are glossy dark bronze-green on top and rich burgundy-purple beneath, a striking two-tone leaf that flashes purple whenever a breeze or handling turns the foliage over. Native to Papua New Guinea, it has a more upright, narrower leaf silhouette than the broader-leaved alocasias, giving it a distinctive, almost architectural presence in a shaded tropical planting or grouped houseplant display. Provide consistent warmth and high humidity, protect from direct sun, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings to avoid rot at the rhizome.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; fern-leaf philodendron climbs readily and develops its most deeply divided leaves when given vertical support.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; fern-leaf philodendron climbs readily and develops its most deeply divided leaves when given vertical support. Mature leaves are cut into numerous narrow, finger-like segments radiating from a central point, giving the plant a delicate, feathery, fern-like texture that sets it dramatically apart from the broad, solid leaves typical of most philodendrons, with new leaves unfurling a coppery bronze before deepening to green. Native to Brazilian rainforests, it climbs steadily up a moss pole or trellis, and taller, more mature plants produce progressively larger and more finely divided leaves than young specimens. Keep humidity high, provide bright indirect light, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings to prevent root rot.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Warszewicz's philodendron is a self-heading (non-climbing) species that needs no moss pole or trellis.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Warszewicz's philodendron is a self-heading (non-climbing) species that needs no moss pole or trellis. Deeply pinnately lobed leaves resemble an oak leaf blown up to dramatic scale, with narrow, finger-like divisions radiating from a strong central rib, giving this Central American species a bold, sculptural silhouette distinct from the smoother, heart-shaped leaves of many common philodendrons. Its non-vining, upright rosette habit stays compact and self-supporting even as leaves grow quite large, making it a striking floor or tabletop specimen without the need for a climbing support. Provide bright indirect light for the best leaf division and size, wipe dust from the deeply cut leaves periodically, and water when the top inch of potting mix has dried.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Mayoi philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more deeply lobed leaves with vertical support.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Mayoi philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more deeply lobed leaves with vertical support. Slender, deeply three-lobed leaves have a gently ruffled, wavy margin and a narrow, elongated central lobe that give the foliage a wispy, almost windswept look distinct from the broader, rounder leaves of related climbing philodendrons. A relatively recent introduction to cultivation from Brazil, it has become popular with collectors for its fine texture and manageable size compared to some of the larger deeply lobed philodendron species, climbing steadily up a support without becoming unwieldy. Keep humidity moderate to high, provide bright indirect light, and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, groundcover, or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Burle Marx philodendron spreads by short rhizomes into a low, clumping groundcover rather than climbing.

directions: Grow as a houseplant, groundcover, or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Burle Marx philodendron spreads by short rhizomes into a low, clumping groundcover rather than climbing. Named for the celebrated Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx, this hybrid produces glossy, elongated, arrow-shaped leaves on a compact, spreading plant that forms a dense, low groundcover in a shaded tropical bed in frost-free climates, or an easy-care rosette in a container further north. Its rhizomatous, non-vining habit makes it useful for filling in beneath larger shade plants or trailing gently over a container's edge, needing no staking or climbing support to look full. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, divide the spreading rhizome to propagate or control size, and protect from any frost.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Silver Sword philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more elongated leaves with vertical support.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Silver Sword philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more elongated leaves with vertical support. Narrow, elongated, arrowhead-shaped leaves have a matte, silvery-blue-green cast and a soft, almost velvety sheen, a cool, muted coloring that stands out among the mostly solid green or variegated philodendrons more commonly grown. A selection of Philodendron hastatum, it climbs steadily up a moss pole, producing progressively larger, more elongated silvery leaves as the vine matures, and its understated, elegant color makes it a popular choice for a minimalist or monochromatic plant display. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the silvery sheen, keep humidity moderate to high, and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall in mild-winter climates, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; yellow sarson is grown as a quick-maturing cool-season crop for both its greens and oilseed.

directions: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall in mild-winter climates, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; yellow sarson is grown as a quick-maturing cool-season crop for both its greens and oilseed. This South Asian mustard type produces bright yellow flowers on branching stems, and its distinctive yellow, rather than brown or black, seed is the traditional source of high-quality mustard oil used across northern India and pressed for cooking, along with young leaves harvested for the classic dish sarson ka saag. Fast-growing and adapted to cool weather, it bolts and sets seed quickly once days lengthen and warm, so plant it early enough to establish good leaf growth before it flowers if greens are the primary goal. Harvest leaves young and often for eating, or allow plants to flower and set seed pods for a home-scale oilseed or seed-saving crop, threshing dried pods once they turn brown and brittle.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
